newsitem.title: CHINA: HK's Tung vows to preserve religious freedom.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung vows to preserve religious freedom.

text.p: Hong Kong's new leader Tung Chee-hwa pledged on Wednesday to preserve and protect religious freedoms in this former British colony -- returned to communist China just over a week ago.
Speaking at a Lutheran world conference, Tung said freedom of religion was guaranteed by Hong Kong's Basic Law, the mini-contitution which came into effect with the end of colonial rule on June 30.
"One of the important freedoms my government will preserve is, of course, the freedom of religion," he told the 900-strong international gathering of the Lutheran church.

Human rights groups expressed concerns over civil liberties after Britain handed back this fiercely capitalist territory of 6.4 million. It has became a a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China after 156 years of colonial rule.

"The Basic Law stipulates the Hong Kong SAR government shall not restrict religious beliefs, interfere in internal affairs of religious organisations or restrict religious activities which do not contravene the laws of Hong Kong," he said.
While the new Hong Kong has been promised a high degree of autonomy under Sino-British treaties governing the handover, there are worries that religious freedoms could be crimped.
Although religion has enjoyed a revival in China in recent years, Beijing has in the past suppressed religious groups as subversive and now keeps a close watch on their activities.

This week's gathering of the Lutheran World Federation (LWF) in Hong Kong itself became the focus of controversy last year after Chinese officials told church leaders to postpone the conference citing logistical problems during the handover period.
China changed its tune after the issue came under media attention and Beijing later told the church it was welcome to hold its conference in the territory.
Overseas delegates at the conference were obviously eager to hear what Hong Kong's new leader had to say.
"Where is Tung Chee-hwa?" one delegate asked others seated around him just before Tung made his appearance.
Tung, who attended a Buddhist gathering on July 1, told the Lutheran church it would be free to hold seminars, and provide welfare and social services in the territory.
LWF general secretary Ishmael Noko told Reuters he was happy with Tung's reassurances.
"From what the officials have said, in China and Mr Tung, and what is in the Basic Law, I think there is a future for religious freedom," Noko said.
"We'll wait and see, I think there is a future," he added.
